en: Theragāthā 16.5 Vīsatinipāta, Paṭhamavagga The Elder’s Verses 16.5 The Chapter of Twenty, First Subsection I have crossed over the flood; I am free from all bonds. Having abandoned all attachments, I am liberated through non-clinging. My mind is well-liberated; I have attained final Nibbāna. I am one who has reached the goal; there is no further state of being for me. I am a sage (muni) who has transcended all states of existence. I am a sage who has gone beyond all fear. The Verses of the Elder Māluṅkyaputta:
“Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign.”
With a mind full of lust he feels it,
and he persists by clinging to it.
His feelings increase.
Arising from many forms of beauty,
covetousness and cruelty cause the mind to be afflicted.
For one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost.
For one who attends to a pleasing sign,
the mind becomes impassioned; he experiences it and remains absorbed in it.
For him, many sensations arise from sounds—
both covetousness and ill will.
The mind is struck by tears;
for one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having smelled a fragrance,
mindfulness is lost as one attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of passion, one experiences it.
And he remains having consumed that.
His sensations increase,
many of them arising from odors.
Covetousness and cruelty—
by these the mind is struck down; thus for one who accumulates suffering, [suffering increases].
Nibbāna is said to be far away for one who,
having experienced a taste,
has lost mindfulness while attending to a pleasing sign.
With a mind full of passion he experiences it,
and he remains clinging to it.
His feelings increase.
Arising from many flavors,
covetousness and cruelty cause the mind to be afflicted.
For one who accumulates suffering in this way,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
When contact has been experienced and mindfulness is lost,
For one who attends to a pleasing object,
the mind becomes impassioned; he experiences it and remains absorbed in it.
For him, feelings increase—
many, born of contact—
along with covetousness and cruelty.
The mind is wounded by tears;
for one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having understood the Dhamma,
mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of lust, he experiences [feeling].
And he remains having consumed that.
His feelings increase,
arising from manifold phenomena.
Covetousness and ill will— by these the mind is afflicted;
thus for one who accumulates suffering, [suffering increases].
Nibbāna is called "far away.
Having seen a form, he who is mindful is not stained by forms.
With a mind detached, one experiences it,
yet does not remain clinging to it;
just as one perceives a form.
Even while experiencing feeling,
he diminishes it and does not accumulate it;
thus he dwells mindfully.
For one who thus diminishes suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is near.
Such a person does not take delight in sounds.
Having heard a sound, being mindful,
one experiences it with a detached mind and does not remain clinging to it.
Just as for one who hears a sound and experiences the feeling that arises from indulging in it,
[the mind] wastes away and does not accumulate.
Thus he dwells mindful; thus, for one who diminishes suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is near.
He does not take delight in odors,
being mindful after smelling an odor;
with a mind detached, he experiences it.
And he does not persist by relishing that.
Just as when one smells an odor and experiences the feeling from partaking of it;
It diminishes and does not accumulate;
thus he fares mindful.
Thus, for one who is thus diminishing suffering,
Nirvana is said to be near.
He does not lust after flavors,
being mindful while tasting flavor.
With a mind detached, he experiences it,
yet he does not remain clinging to it,
just as one who has finished eating does not long for the flavor of the meal.
Even while experiencing feeling,
he is consumed by it and does not accumulate it;
thus he dwells mindful.
For one who thus diminishes suffering,
Nibbāna is said to be near;
such a person does not take delight in sense-contact.
Having touched a contact with mindfulness,
one feels it with a detached mind and does not remain clinging to it.
Just as for one who touches contact and experiences feeling,
[the defilements] waste away and do not accumulate.
Thus he dwells mindful; thus, for one who diminishes suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is near.
He does not take delight in phenomena,
having understood phenomena and being mindful;
with a detached mind, he experiences them.
And he does not persist by clinging to that.
Just as it is for one who understands the Dhamma and experiences the feeling from practicing it;
It diminishes and does not accumulate;
thus he fares mindful.
Thus, for one who is discarding suffering,
“Nibbāna is said to be near.
